image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted distribution / density-style area chart** (filled histogram-like distribution curves).
- Two panels compare temperature distributions for **1951–1980** and **2013–2023**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: two vertically stacked panels, one for each time period.
- **Overlay**: in the lower panel, the earlier **1951–1980 base-period** distribution appears again as a light hatched reference behind the newer distribution.
- **Color segmentation**: the distribution is divided into labeled temperature categories (extremely cold, cold, normal, hot, extremely hot) using different colors.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Summer temperature category / anomaly class (Extremely cold, Cold, Normal, Hot, Extremely hot) | Ordinal | Position along x-axis; color/hue of filled area; text labels along bottom |
| Frequency / relative occurrence | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; height of filled distribution area |
| Time period (1951–1980, 2013–2023) | Temporal | Faceting into two vertical panels; large panel labels |
| Base-period reference (1951–1980) | Temporal | Overlaid light gray hatched distribution in both panels; annotation label |

1. What do you notice?
	In the first graph , from 1951-1980, I noticed that the normal, cold, and hot temperature was almost evenly distributed, relative to the months. There was little to no frequency for extremely hot and cold temperatures. On the other hand, in the graph of 2013-2023, I noticed that hot temperatures were the most common, and the frequency of extremely hot went up by a lot, while the frequency of normal and cold temperatures went substantially down. 
2. What do you wonder?
	I wonder why this significant change occurred. Was it due to the significant increase of fossil fuels and global warming? Also, what is considered the “normal” temperature, and how is it determined? Did the idea of what is considered extremely hot and extremely cold change over time?
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
	This impacts my community because just last december, there were days where the temperature was above 50. This is abnormal, especially in December, and I wonder if it will be considered normal in a few years due to the trend the graphs are showing. Also, global warming is a prevalent issue in our community, which is obvious from the graphs, and we really need to do something about it. 
4. What’s going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
	Temperature is on the rise!

comments.raw_comment: Heightened Summer Heat: I notice that as time increases, and therefore comes closer to current day, the average temperature increases as well. From 1951-1980, the distribution of summer temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere was approximately normally distributed with the majority of days within the “normal” temperature range. However from 2013-2023, the graph has drastically shifted to the right with the majority of days in the “hot” and “extremely hot” temperature categories. This graph is right skewed. The first graph spans over 29 years while the second only shows data from a ten year period. I wonder, if the graphs were created on a ten year basis (for example, 1991-2001, 2002-2012, 2013-2023) would the graphs change as dramatically? I wonder what major inventions have led to this climate change? Could it include farming, cars, increased production? I wonder, is this data reflected similarly from other nations? Does this data match that of the southern hemisphere? I also am wondering, what specific temperatures constitute the categories “cold, normal, hot, and extremely hot”? As a New Hampshire resident, this directly impacts me and my community through our climate. The data shows summer temperatures of the Northern Hemisphere are increasingly warming up, impacting our lives in the summer. This climate change does not just impact what clothes we wear in the summer, it impacts available water, food availability, and even power use/consumption.

Miles Borne

1. What do you notice?
I notice 2 graphs that appear approximately normal distribution. On the bottom, there is a scale of temperatures that shows cold, Normal, and hot. It appears that in the graph of 1951-1980, there is an equal distribution of temperatures that are cold and hot. I wonder how the temperature changes from year to year. Is it in a linear fashion changing the same every year? Or in an exponential fashion, starting slowly and then rapidly increasing?

Also in the summer, this place is really lovely but because of how hot it’s getting there are simply some days where you shouldn’t go outside that often because of how hot it is.

These graphs show how the average summer land temperatures across the northern hemisphere have changed over the past 72 years (1951-2023). In the first graph (1951-1980), it is apparent that normal temperatures occur most often. However, cold and hot temperatures are both still very frequent and their frequencies are just about equal. Extremely cold and extremely hot temperatures are very rare during this time period. In the second graph (2013-2023) cold and even normal temperatures become significantly less frequent than they once were, and extremely cold temperatures are very rare. On the other hand, hot temperatures become more frequent, and extremely hot temperatures which were basically nonexistent in the first graph become much more common. I wonder why the graphs are such different shapes. The first graph is very high and narrow while the second graph is lower and wider. I can infer that this difference in temperatures is due to the range of the data because the second graph has a wider range of temperatures included in it. I wonder if climate change will continue to progress until the majority of temperatures are extremely hot. What will we do to stop this from happening? 
"You Are Going to Need More than a Fan this Summer"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that average summer temperatures in Northern Hemisphere have increased significantly since the 1950s. Over a mere ten year period (2013-2023), the average summer temperature rose to be in the "hot" rather than "normal" range. Interestingly, the graphs have also changed in terms of distribution. The data points are more extreme, leading to a wider curve. Also, the Northern Hemisphere now experiences "extremely hot" weather, when from 1951-1980 this was virtually nonexistent. 

I wonder if climate change has precipitated these changes. Anthropogenic activity is known to cause more extreme weather patterns, so I am curious if the wide distribution of temperature from 2013-2023 has the same cause. I also wonder if "normal" temperatures are in the context of the Earth's history, or simply 1951-1980. Is it normal for the preindustrial era, too?

This relates to me and my community because rising summer temperatures makes the Northern Hemisphere less hospitable, especially for those with existing medical conditions. If extremely hot temperatures persist, people might be encouraged to migrate toward the cooler poles. Rising temperatures could also hurt species diversity, as natives might not be able to survive in different conditions.

"A Midsummer Night's HEAT"

This graph depicts the temperature of the northern hemisphere from July to August from 1950 until 2023. The graph compares how the temperature rates have gradually changed over time. In the 1951 to 1980 time period, there was a much higher rate of moderate temperatures. Cold and hot temperature rates of frequency were pretty even. However, from 2013 to 2023, the hot temperature spanning into extremely hot temperatures has become more common. In present days, cold and neutral temperatures are becoming rare in the northern hemisphere. With the effects of global warming at hand, many activist groups fight for ways to end the harm humans are doing to Earth which has made temperatures scarily increase. Yet, if their efforts are implemented will they work? Will temperatures start to drop again? Or are global warming and the extremely hot temperatures unwavering from irreversible damage? This relates to my community because we all are negatively affected by increasing temperatures. The reservoir by my home that has been used by the public for decades has been closed the past few summers because of dangerous algae blooms caused by extremely hot temperatures. Many people in the area, without even swimming, have gotten sick from these blooms. 
“Up Next: Only Hot Days Ahead”

1) I notice that summer temperatures from 2013-2023 are less cold and more hot, even treading to extremely hot compared to temperatures in 1951-1980, where they were fairly split between cold and hot. Looking at the graphs we can see this clearly as the graph from 1951-1980 is more centered and has no tails while the graph from 2013-2023 has a left tail and therefore is skewed to the left, which in this case it means more hot temperatures during the summer.

2) I wonder the extent global warming has been affecting these higher temperatures during the summer and what this means moving forward as our planet becomes hotter and hotter. How will this impact us who are being subjected to extremely hot temperatures healthwise? How long until our environment is damaged and what can we do to reverse it, if there is anything?

3) This relates to me and my community because summer In New York is approaching right around the corner. Even though we are still in early May, the temperatures are already starting to warm----to the 70s and even 80s. On those days, it's so hot that it feels like summer has already come. If it already feels like this in spring, then imagine when summer actually comes.

4) Summer Surge: Temperatures At An All-Time High

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that in the first graph showing the temperatures for 1951-1980 had a peak in the normal temperature range and had a minuscule amount of extremely hot days. In the second graph showing the temperatures for 2013-2023, the graph had a peak in the hot temperature range and around ⅔ of the temperatures for that time period were within the extremely hot range. I noticed that as more years passed, the hotter the days got during the summertime. I wonder where in the Northern Hemisphere these temperatures were recorded, because there is a difference in temperatures during the summer months in New England compared to somewhere like Florida or Texas. I would also wonder what role climate change has had on these temperatures and if there are any correlations between the increasing temperatures during certain summers and the rate of climate change. I also wonder what the graphs define as a “normal”, “extremely hot”, “hot”,  or “cold” temperature. There is no numerical value provided for each category, just a description which can be interpreted differently by each person. With rising temperatures each summer this can have an impact on the environment and the people. With the rising temperatures this can change rainfall patterns which impacts the plants and animals around us during the summer. Severe increases in temperatures will increase the evaporation rates which will create longer and more severe droughts for communities. 
“Climate Change: Weather You Like it or Not”

1. While looking at the graphs I notice that  over the past 72 years the average summer land temperatures have gone from cold to hot then extremely hot. From 1950 to 1980, the temperature of the lands varied from cold, hot, and extremely hot. However in 2020 the graph shows that there is about a 80% increase in the hottere days. The 1951-1980 graph has a normal distribution with the temperatures being around the mean of 1 degree celsius above the baseline. Comparing the tails of the graph shows a trend that is going on. The upper extreme of  2 degrees celsius from 1951-1980 is now in the bulk of the 2013-2023 distribution. 
2. This is concerning seeing how much hotter it is getting by the years. I wonder how they determined what is extremely hot and what is normal. I wonder what can we do if anything to slow down these increasing temperatures and what is influencing them to increase at such a rapid rate. 
3. This has an impact on our community because as the years go by and the temperature gets hotter, it can affect future generations. Such an increase in temperature can put a lot of nature at risk and habitats for wildlife.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed the temperatures during 1951-1980 in the Northern Hemisphere had a somewhat even split between cold, normal, and hot. This pattern took a drastic change from 2013-2023 when the whole graph shifted to the right. This shift increased the hot and extremely hot days but lessened the cold and normal days. I wonder how this graph will look in the next ten years, and if anything is being done to battle this. The increase in extremely hot temperatures affects my community tremendously. It is not good for our Earth to be facing such hot temperatures and no regulation with cold/normal temperatures. With the temperatures so high, it increases the chance of drought, plants dying, and heat exhaustion for humans. All these factors decrease our ability to thrive in our community. The title I came up with: “Sizzling Stats: the harsh truth about our days!"

I noticed that in the second graph, there are significantly more scorching temperatures than in the first, which means that the temperatures are increasing very fast. 
I noticed that the summer temperatures depict the June-July-August range.
I wonder why the temperatures are rising so quickly.
I also wonder if the rest of the world is also facing the same temperature issues to the same degree.
I wonder why the data collected was only in the Northern Hemisphere. Was it too difficult to also collect similar data in the Southern Hemisphere during the base period?
Increasing temperatures due to climate change can lead to a multitude of challenges for both humans and the environment we live in. In communities around the world, extreme heat events can pose health risks, such as the elderly, children, and those with pre-existing health conditions. Rising temperatures can also exacerbate issues like drought, water scarcity, and wildfires, impacting agriculture, biodiversity, and overall ecosystem health. Additionally, warmer temperatures can contribute to the melting of polar ice caps and glaciers, leading to sea level rise and coastal erosion, which threatens coastal communities and infrastructure. Addressing the impacts of rising temperatures requires concerted efforts at both local and global levels, including mitigation strategies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adaptation measures to build resilience to the changes already underway.
Climate Change is Going to Kill Us All!

The first thing I notice is how many "Extremely hot" days there are in the 2013-2023 graph. The extremely hot category is barely noticeable in the 1951-1980 base period. It would mean that the hottest days of today didn't even exist back then. The extremely cold category also reaches out a little further in the 2013-2023 graph, meaning there's some evidence that even the coldest days of today were a little worse than before. 
I wonder if 30 years before the 1951-1980 base period were any cooler. It might help provide some context to the graph we see. I imagine prior to 1951 wasn't that much cooler, but it would still be nice to see it compared to 1951-1980. Another thing I wonder is why the data collected was only in the Northern Hemisphere. Was it too difficult to also collect similar data in the Southern Hemisphere during the base period?
This relates to me personally since as the days get hotter in our modern world we all generally suffer more for it. The extremely hot days mean were more at risk for dangerous wildfires (and other fires) since the majority of terrain is so dry for a long period of the year due to the extreme heat. We have to think of ways to adapt in order to cope with the fact our world is hotter. A good name for the graph would be: "Days Are Hotter Today Compared to 30 to 50 Years Ago", or "The Cost of Living In the Modern World: Extreme Heat."

Interesting title: Visualizing the Alarming Rise in Northern Hemisphere Summer Temperatures

The two area graphs provide a striking visual comparison of summer temperature distributions in the Northern Hemisphere across different 30-year periods, revealing an alarming warming trend. The 1951-1980 graph approximates a normal distribution, with temperatures symmetrically clustered around the mean of 1°C above baseline. Fast forward to 2013-2023, and the curve has shifted significantly to the right and flattened out, with the peak now around 1.5°C above baseline. From living in San Luis Obispo, California, I've witnessed the changing climate firsthand, with summers growing hotter and more prolonged.
Comparing the tails reveals an alarming trend: the former upper extreme of 2°C from 1951-1980 is now squarely in the bulk of the 2013-2023 distribution. In San Luis Obispo, we've experienced the consequences, from severe droughts to extended wildfire seasons. Graphs like these make the reality of climate change starkly visible, underscoring the urgency of addressing this warming trend. They remind us of the need for our community to take action and build a more sustainable future.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice from the graphs that the frequency of "normal" temperatures has severely decreased in the last 72 years. I've noticed that what was considered a hot average temperature from 1951-1980 has now become what is the norm in the Northern Hemisphere. I also noticed that there is much more variability in the graph now. In the base period the temperatures were heavily centered at the normal temperature with small tails on both sides. While in the modern plot the ranges of temperatures is much greater with a very large right tail insinuating that there are much higher temperatures now than there was then. 

I wonder why the shape of the plot has changed and not just the temperatures itself. Knowing about global warming and the production of fossil fuels, the temperature increase does not surprise me but the idea that the distributions are different shapes is puzzling. I wonder if that can be attributed to exponential growth. I also wonder how the Northern Hemisphere compares to the southern hemisphere and if there are similar trends there or if possibly they are opposite trends. 

This relates to my community because from a few environmental classes I've taken, I learned that this massive temperature increase is putting a lot of nature at risk and making habitats and species die. As someone who loves to travel and see nature it is important to me that the animals and plants around us are being taken care of by us.

The graph displaying the Northern Hemisphere temperatures from 1951-1980 appears to follow a normal distribution, where cold and hot temperatures seem to be evenly distributed on both sides. This indicates just how quickly temperature is evolving to be hotter and hotter and will continue to do so over time.

3. These increasing temperatures severely impact our community as the earth will continue to heat up and affect our future generations. I'm concerned about how high the temperature will be for my future kids and grandkids and how that will impact their lifestyle.

comments.raw_comment:
Watching the animation the first thing that became clear was that when comparing 1951-1980 to 2013-2023 the number of hot and extremely hot days has dramatically increased, while at the same time, there is a substantial reduction of cold days. This is because over time the curve not only became shorter and wider but experienced a left shift. This indicates that the median temperature went from being “Normal” in the ’50s to being “Hot” in modern times. 
I'm curious exactly how this data was recorded. The subtitle says it is the temperature in the Northern Hemisphere, so is it fair to assume it is an average of every country’s or every state/province’s temperature? Additionally, I am curious as to the exact range of temperatures that constitute each temperature label. To me hot is any temperature over 80 degrees, but I wonder if they used a more conservative scale with hot starting at 90 degrees. This applies to me since I live in an area particularly susceptible to fires. Higher temperatures mean dryer brush and higher fire risk, which directly impacts my community's and my safety. I would title this graph “Rising Temperatures Means Sweltering Summers.”

comments.raw_comment:
Interesting title: Visualizing the Alarming Rise in Northern Hemisphere Summer Temperatures

The two area graphs provide a striking visual comparison of summer temperature distributions in the Northern Hemisphere across different 30-year periods, revealing an alarming warming trend. The 1951-1980 graph approximates a normal distribution, with temperatures symmetrically clustered around the mean of 1°C above baseline. Fast forward to 2013-2023, and the curve has shifted significantly to the right and flattened out, with the peak now around 1.5°C above baseline. From living in San Luis Obispo, California, I've witnessed the changing climate firsthand, with summers growing hotter and more prolonged.
Comparing the tails reveals an alarming trend: the former upper extreme of 2°C from 1951-1980 is now squarely in the bulk of the 2013-2023 distribution. In San Luis Obispo, we've experienced the consequences, from severe droughts to extended wildfire seasons. Graphs like these make the reality of climate change starkly visible, underscoring the urgency of addressing this warming trend. They remind us of the need for our community to take action and build a more sustainable future.

Additionally, other consequences regarding money, such as for more energy for air conditioning and for more water may arise from this increase in temperature.

As I study the graphs, I can't help but notice a significant change in how summer temperatures have evolved over time. Back in the 1950s to 1980s, the temperature distribution was like a symphony, with most of the notes clustered around the "Normal" range. It felt like summers followed a predictable rhythm during that era. But fast forward to 2013-2023, and it's like the music has changed entirely. The peak has shifted to "Hot," and there's this long, drawn-out crescendo reaching into "Extremely hot" temperatures. It's like summers have become more unpredictable, with heatwaves becoming the new norm.

I wonder what's behind this dramatic shift. What's causing this sudden change in temperature patterns? Is it something we're doing, or is it nature's own rhythm? I'm also curious about how different parts of the Northern Hemisphere are experiencing these changes. Are some places feeling the heat more intensely than others?

This shift to hotter summers has real consequences for us because it means farmers might struggle with crops, and we might find ourselves cranking up the air conditioning more often, leading to higher electricity bills. And let's not forget the health risks, especially for those who are vulnerable to extreme heat. 

These graphs paint a picture of a world where summers are getting hotter, and it's up to us to tune in and take action.  A catchy headline could be "Hotter Summers Ahead: Graphs Sound the Alarm on Temperature Surge in the Northern Hemisphere".

comments.raw_comment: Unfortunately, (although not shockingly) it looks like the summer land temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere have been becoming increasingly warmer over the past 72 years. From the animation, I can see that the land temperatures between 1951-1980 were normally distributed around “normal” temperatures, as described in the graphic. However, as the time periods move further, the distribution of summer temperatures start centering moving toward “hot” temperatures. I wonder what “cold”, “normal”, “hot”, etc. temperatures actually are. Are they measured in degrees Fahrenheit or Celsius? What do “normal” temperatures mean? As someone who is definitely concerned about the effects of global warming, this graphic really scares me! With land temperatures increasing, who knows what will happen to our world, namely our biodiversity. Especially in California! This state is one of the most diverse regions in both abiotic and biotic realms. What dangers does California face with these increasing temperatures? I just wonder what people in my community and myself can do in this situation, especially since this change in temperatures is mostly due to the acceleration in greenhouse gas emissions specifically from larger corporations. The visualisation illustrates the shift in the summer temperature pattern of the Northern hemisphere across the intensity of heat levels, for identified year-slices. The distribution follows a normal curve, yet the extremely hot period is experienced in 2013-2023 year-slice is the highest across years with the cold slice drastically reduced. The frequency of the temperature has also reduced with the new entrant category - extremely hot. The visual also indicates that before 1991, the mean/median temperature  was 'normal' and now is in the hot category (new normal).
I wonder if these measurements are taken at the same geo-location, at the same spot (with/without tree coverage), every time at the specified time (always say at 11am), across the years, in the indicated months. What instruments were used to capture and the metric adopted. What is the benchmark of cold, normal, hot and extremely hot. How did we manage to get the same number (assumption) of data points at each of these locations across years.
It is important to understand the landscape changes, the foliage coverage, the habitation growth, the construction/developments, usage of glass/solar panels/tar/cement in the vicinity etc, presence/absence/disappearance of water bodies - that have contributed to the rise in the temperature. This can help us work on ideas/strategies to bring down the temperature impact in the local areas.

After examining the graph, I notice that as the years increase, the average summer land temperatures across the Northern Hemisphere are getting hotter and hotter. In the graph from 1951 to 1980, the summer temperatures are normally distributed. In comparison, the graph for the years 2013 to 2023 is skewed right. This tells us that for the years 2013 to 2023, summer temperatures have gotten much hotter than compared to past years. 
	I wonder why summer temperatures have gotten so much hotter compared between the years 1951 to 1980 and 2013 to 2023. What is the main reason for such an increase in temperature? Is it because more carbon emissions are being released? Is this due to the agricultural industry? The industrial industry? Are there less trees? I am curious to know why temperatures are rising as fast as they are and what the leading cause for it is. 
	This relates to me and my community because we live in the northern hemisphere, so we are directly and physically feeling the temperatures this data is illustrating. Based on my personal experience, the data from this graph is definitely true. As each summer goes by, it seems like each one is getting hotter and hotter. Additionally, being from California, I have experienced living in a drought for many years and it truly puts into perspective how critical this rise in heat is. 
	A catchy headline for the graph’s main idea is “Warm to Boiling: This Summer is Going to be Fire”.

What Do You Notice?

I noticed that the use of color is very convenient and on theme for the context of this visualization. I also appreciate the use a density plot to illustrate the message. It highlights how summer temperatures are becoming warmer due to the right distribution shift. The old mean temperature used to fall under normal, however, after a couple of years, temperatures have increased which is why the new mean summer temperature is now categorized as hot. It's also really convenient that the new distribution was plotted on top of the previous one as it shows how much temperatures have shifted.

What Do You Wonder?

I wonder if this trend is similar to that of the southern hemisphere and the tropics. How much different are the changes? Which hemisphere has the most severe shift?

How Does This Relate To You and Your Community?

This relates to me and my community since  we are the main contributors to rising temperatures. Human activity contributes a lot to global warming which in turn, not only affects all human communities, but all living things on earth as well. Wild fires, for example, have caused destruction to many humans and animals. However, these wild fires are intensified and sometimes even caused by extreme temperatures.

Hot Girl Summer? See The Trend Of Rising Summer Temperatures

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed was the colors used to represent the different summer temperatures in the graph. I thought it was really cool how warmer colors were used to represent warmer temperatures and cooler colors were used to represent cooler temperatures. This made the graph much easier to interpret for me. I also appreciated the moving graphic below which illustrated summer temperature changes over time. Such movement made it easier to tell that the majority of summer temperatures seemed to be increasing significantly over time. 

I wonder what factors are contributing to the observed increase in summer temperatures? Is it primarily due to human activities such as greenhouse gas emissions, or are there natural factors at play as well? I also wonder what the potential impacts of rising summer temperatures are. How might they affect ecosystems, agriculture, human health, and infrastructure?

These rising temperatures have a significant impact on my society. To start, increasing temperatures can lead to more frequent and intense heatwaves, which can cause heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion and heatstroke. Vulnerable populations, including the elderly, children, and those with pre-existing health conditions, are particularly at risk. Additionally, rising temperatures can worsen air quality and increase the spread of vector-borne diseases, impacting public health.

Title: The Summer Sizzle

The thing I notice is that this is the most effective visualization I have seen since looking at these graphs. The dark red getting more prevalent in the gif as time goes on is extremely striking. Further, the shift from a pretty normal distribution in 1951 to the right skew in 2013 is jarring. These two elements combined make this graph incredibly effective at portraying how summer temperatures have gotten hotter.

I wonder why this was limited to the Northern Hemisphere. The largest reason I can think of is that most NYT readers are likely in the United States, if not the Northern Hemisphere. However, from what I know this is a global issue. I know that summer in Australia and Brazil have also been getting much hotter. When clicking the citation, the data is available for the whole globe.  Was this done to make the visualization more striking? Was it done by NYT editors to keep their readers in mind?

This relates to me and my community as I can anecdotally verify the truth of this. I am from Los Angeles and throughout high school I worked at a day camp and my last two years were marked by extreme heat advisories. It would be so hot, that it was literally unsafe for us to bring our campers outside for anything besides going in the pool. This graph serves a powerful way to convey my experience to people from other parts of North America which are not subject to this extreme heat.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing that I noticed about this graph is that temperatures are rapidly increasing over time. In the first graph that is showing summer temperatures from 1951 to 1980, there is barely any red in the visual indicating extremely hot temperatures. However, there is a very large portion of the visual for 2013-2023 showing extremely hot temperatures, indicating that summer temperatures are increasing over time. The 2013 to 2023 time frame also has an alarmingly low portion of the graph that has normal or cold temperatures-- extreme values are much more common. I wonder what the actual temperatures are recorded on the x-axis. What temperature exactly qualifies as "extremely hot", and how does that compare to my own perception of what is "hot" or "cold"? This graph relates to me and my community because the topic of global warming is widely discussed today, and is becoming an increasingly pressing issue. As a young adult, I am part of the community that will be inheriting the world as we know it, and it is our job to take care of the planet that we live on before we cause even further destruction. I myself have noticed more extreme weather than I did when I was a little kid, 100 degree days are much more common than they used to be. Additionally, in California we have experienced severe droughts more often than we should. A catchy headline for this graph would be "It's Getting Hot in Here- Rising Temperatures Over Time".

These prove to be just a couple of things that contribute to global warming and how out-of-control it has become.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that over time summer temperatures have increased drastically. More specifically we observe how from 1951 to 2023 the changes in the frequency of different temperatures and the hotter temperatures are now more common. Since 1951 the most frequent among the Summer temperatures from June to August in the Northern Hemisphere was a normal temperature. However, in the present day that's changed to a hot temperature. Then in regards to the extremes back in 1951-1980, both extremely hot and extremely cold were such small portions of the graphic. In the present day both of these extremes have changed the extremely cold portion has managed to get smaller while Extremely hot has become a significant portion of the summer temperatures even becoming the second most common temperature. I wonder what many effects have contributed to this significant increase in Summer Temperatures. I would also like to know how these temperatures were recorded since it's not said by the graphic and whether it's taking the averages. This graphic can show effectively just how significant the increase in temperature has been over the past 72 years. It is a sign of concern for Earth's inhabitants as it shows past trends and ultimately gets you thinking of future trends. It makes you think of how dire the situation of global warming is and how we need to act now to try and prevent such increases from continuing. A fitting title would be: "Heating Hemisphere: Increasing Temperatures from 1950 to 2023."
